title: Basa-Jauna and the Three Brothers
subtitle: A wild-man household in a Basque story

learningObjectives.text: How do the three brothers fare?

wildman.author: Basque storytellers; collected and translated by Wentworth Webster
wildman.translator: Wentworth Webster, with assistance from Julien Vinson and other local contributors
wildman.locator: BASA-JAUNA, THE WILD MAN.; BASA-JAUNA, THE WILD MAN., normalized characters 1091-1635
wildman.excerpt: the three brothers set out together. At eight o'clock in the evening they come to a grand castle, and they knock at the door, and the Basa-Andre (wild woman) comes to answer. She asks: "Who is there?" And they reply, "It is we who are here." "What do you want, young children? Where are you going to at this time of night?" "We ask and beg of you to give us shelter for to-night; we will be satisfied with a corner of the floor, poor wretches as we are." "I have my husband, the Basa-Jaun, and if he catches you he will eat you; that's certain.
wildman.note: Verbatim English text from Webster's second edition, collected chiefly in Labourd. The collection distinguishes local tales from French-derived contes des fées and compares some motifs with wider European stories.

narrativeBlocks.title: The wild man of the woods
narrativeBlocks.body: Basa-Jauna is the Basque wild man — the shaggy, mountain-dwelling lord of the flocks who knows the secrets of the wild. His mate is Basa-Andre, the wild woman — equally powerful, often more dangerous.

narrativeBlocks.title: The three brothers go in
narrativeBlocks.body: Three brothers go up into the mountains and one by one encounter the wild couple — the elder two fail or flee, but the youngest, who treats the wild ones rightly, wins their favour.

narrativeBlocks.title: The secret of the wild
narrativeBlocks.body: The wild man's secret is the land's knowledge — where the flocks go, what the mountains hide — and he shares it only with the courteous.

narrativeBlocks.title: Basa-Andre's danger
narrativeBlocks.body: The wild woman is the tale's edge: beautiful and deadly, she lures the unwary — the youngest brother survives because he keeps his wits and his manners both.

narrativeBlocks.title: The wild couple's meaning
narrativeBlocks.body: Basa-Jauna and Basa-Andre are the mountains themselves made person: generous to the respectful shepherd, fatal to the arrogant — the Pyrenees' own mythology.
